claims.claim: The strategy commits that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented' and teardown 'remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time', while the PRD introduces exactly that: a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) in ApplicationSetStrategy that automates ordered deletion of generated Applications. Both commitments cannot hold.

The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section states 'No immediate Risks to consider', but T-28511 is field evidence against it: an ApplicationSet configuring rollingSync step order with reverse deletion strategy — whose wait-for-full-deletion semantics the PRD defines — gets stuck in an infinite delete/re-create loop when a child Application is stuck Progressing, because the wait never completes and the controller restarts the wave.

T-26271's CI diff failure ('argocd app diff' forbidden as a narrower identity after 'we recently enabled the sync impersonation flag') is the direct consequence of RFC-001's impersonation design: sync privileges are decoupled from control-plane privileges via destinationServiceAccounts, so the server-side apply dry-run runs without the broad cluster-Secret permissions the reporter is chasing. Neither document cites the other.

RFC-001 answers its audit-trail open question only for sync ('kubernetes audit trail events capture both the actual user and the impersonating user'), but T-28695 shows the diff path ignores destinationServiceAccounts and still acts as the standing cluster Secret credential — so after impersonation ships, sync acts and is audited as the tenant service account while diff still acts as the old privileged identity, and the unbounded patch RBAC granted to that credential (with no dry-run verb in Kubernetes RBAC) is real write authority nobody's review process watches.

T-27833 asks for impersonation with a per-resource split — control plane creates namespaces via the Argo CD SA while the impersonated SA, stripped of namespace permissions, performs the sync — but RFC-001 explicitly decides 'the service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level', so the requested control cannot be built on the impersonation design as approved.

T-9095 (respect users' existing Kubernetes RBAC instead of duplicating it in Argo CD) and RFC-001 (manage sync permissions 'using kubernetes native RBAC implementation rather than complex configurations in AppProjects') converge on the same access model from opposite ends — UI actions and sync operations respectively — without citing each other; the governance consequence is that both move the acting identity and the review point from Argo CD RBAC config to cluster RoleBindings.

RFC-002's commit server pushes machine-generated commits into git — the system of record — using a repository-write secret, while stamping the human dry-commit author into the README template and CommitManifests commitAuthor field; T-28239 confirms these hydrated commits are unsigned today, so nothing cryptographically distinguishes the bot's writes from human acts, and Argo CD rejects its own hydrated output where signature verification is enforced. The signing feature that would close this is opt-in and default false.

RFC-002's hydrator turns every dry commit into fresh hydrated commits on the sync branch, and T-27875 shows that a new commit arriving while a sync is in progress leaves automated-sync apps (without selfHeal) OutOfSync indefinitely because Status.Sync.Revision records the last compared, not last synced, revision — hydrated branches will hit this commit-during-sync window routinely, making the hydrator a systematic trigger for the auto-sync stall.

T-26443's stale-manifest sync ('we only observe this when the hydrator runs in push-to-stage mode; the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests') is the operational cost of RFC-002's explicit design choice: push-to-stage 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch' and implementing a promotion system is a stated Non-Goal, so the gap the ticket reports is designed-in, not a regression.

T-27327 proposes that rollback 'directly updates the sync branch (bypassing the staging branch)' in both hydrator modes, which breaks RFC-002's core opinion that change lineage is 'fully represented as a series of dry commit hashes' enabling rules like 'prod may never be more than one dry hash ahead of test' — a rollback commit landing on the sync branch outside the promotion path is exactly the externally-held state the RFC forbids.

T-24578 (Source Hydrator support for ApplicationSets to control destroy ordering across clusters) and the PRD's deletionOrder Reverse describe the same underlying user need — ordered deletion of ApplicationSet-generated Applications — solved by two different mechanisms in two workstreams that never reference each other; the PRD would remove T-24578's stated motivation for the app-of-apps workaround.

The PRD's Reverse deletion 'expects the rollingSync field to have a specified order' and deletes in the reverse of those sequential steps, while T-28755 proposes parallel progressive sync steps (parallel/parallelGroups) with no defined linear order — if both ship, 'reverse of the configured order' is undefined for parallel groups and the two features collide at the same rollingSync field neither proposal reconciles.

RFC-002 resolves external Helm values by recommending the umbrella-chart approach with a single dry source, but T-24417 reports that path fails its users: pointing DrySource at a chart in a Helm repository is impossible, and 'switching to helm dependencies... makes it difficult to use with ApplicationSets to control the chart version across environments' — the RFC's chosen simplification is the exact mechanism the field ticket says does not work.

T-28927 scopes the promotion of Progressive Sync to Stable while the observability needed to validate maturity does not exist: T-27846's requested progressive-sync metrics (time to trigger, per-step duration, why a sync is not starting) are still an open proposal, and T-27949 shows a real rollout-complete-while-OutOfSync failure that produced no evidence because 'controller logs were at warn level, so no relevant progressive-sync transition logs were emitted' — the failure modes blocking Stable are currently unmeasurable in production.

The incident review's interim restriction that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists (each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave) stands directly in the path of two planned workstreams beyond the pilot it was written against: T-24578, which proposes Source Hydrator support for ApplicationSets (progressive sync's own resource), and T-27949's pilot itself, which is already running the hydrator on a RollingSync repository where 'each of those commits is picked up as a source change'.

RFC-001 commits that impersonation 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications', but the platform sync decided rollout goes 'behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide', and T-26271's reporter already describes 'projects where we recently enabled the sync impersonation flag' — the shipped/decided rollout granularity contradicts the approved design's system-level-only switch.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode delegates promotion to an external system by design, T-26443 shows stale stage-branch content gets auto-synced when that promoter lags, and the notes reveal the promoter in question 'is still the shell script, nobody owns it' — an unowned shell script is the single mover between staged and deployed state for every push-to-stage application.

proposals.change: Record the root cause on the ticket: with impersonation enabled, the diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources; the breadth of the cluster Secret credential is irrelevant, so the reporter should stop investigating it.
proposals.citedLine: the CI diff failures (the missing-permissions one, T-26271) got root-caused on the call: with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff. someone should note the root cause on that ticket so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret.

proposals.change: Record that the hydrator rollback work is deprioritized to next quarter, and that the dev pair assigned to it moves to the progressive sync deletion loop.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record the staging reproduction with reverse deletion order and the interim mitigation: per the incident runbook, switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting any child Application, until the controller fix lands.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

proposals.change: Record the confirmed mechanism (each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave) and the interim restriction from the incident review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists.
proposals.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.

deltas.body: Decision: impersonation rolls out behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide, and no project enables it until the diff story is fixed.
deltas.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.

deltas.body: Standing operational rule: before manually deleting any child Application of a progressive-sync ApplicationSet, switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion; this holds until the controller fix for the delete/re-create loop lands.
deltas.citedLine: mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

deltas.body: Interim restriction: hydrator pilot repositories must not use progressive sync until a debounce for hydrator-push wave restarts exists.
deltas.citedLine: interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce.

deltas.body: Open governance item needing an owner: the strategy document's commitment that ApplicationSet deletion stays manual disagrees with the PRD shipping ordered deletion; the contradiction is acknowledged but undecided.
deltas.citedLine: someone asked whether the strategy doc still says appset deletion stays manual — if the PRD ships ordered deletion those two disagree, needs an owner. not deciding here.
